rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Bohr's orbits have angular momentum n h/(2π) and hydrogen energies −13.6/n^2 eV. The electron radiates only in a jump, and the photon energy is the difference of the levels. The Balmer series is the set of jumps that end on n = 2.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
En(H) = −13.6 Z²/n² eV
hν = ΔE
λ = h/(mv) (de Broglie)

rows.text: E_2 = −3.40 eV and E_3 = −1.51 eV.  ·  R is about 1.097 × 10^7 per metre.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Bohr's hydrogen atom keeps a positive nucleus and an electron in orbit, and adds the rule that the angular momentum is n h / (2π). Only integer n is allowed.  ·  In an allowed orbit the electron does not radiate, even though it is accelerating. Radiation happens only when the electron jumps from one allowed energy to a lower one.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Bohr orbits  ·  Energy levels  ·  Balmer series  ·  Photon difference

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Angular momentum is n h / 2π.  ·  The electron does not radiate in an allowed orbit.  ·  A jump emits one photon.  ·  Balmer jumps end on n = 2.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Bohr model: electron in fixed circular orbits; angular momentum mvr = nh/2π; energy En = −13.6 eV·Z²/n² (for H, Z=1).  ·  Rydberg/Balmer series: 1/λ = R(H)(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²). Absorption/emission = ΔE = hν between levels.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: What is the photon energy of a jump?

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: A hydrogen electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2. Find the photon energy. Use E_3 = −1.51 eV and E_2 = −3.40 eV.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: The ground-state energy of hydrogen is → B  ·  The Balmer series ends on → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: The energies are E_n = −13.6 / n^2 electronvolts. The ground state is n = 1, at −13.6 eV. The zero of energy is the electron removed to infinity.  ·  The photon energy is the difference of the two levels. A jump from n = 3 to n = 2 is a Balmer line. Jumps that end on n = 1 are the Lyman series, in the ultraviolet.  ·  The wave formula is 1/λ = R (1/n1^2 − 1/n2^2). R is the Rydberg constant. A larger jump gives a larger photon energy and a shorter wavelength.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ skip the key fact → ✅ bohr model: electron in fixed circular orbits; angular momentum mvr = nh/2π; energy en = −13.6 ev·z²/n² (for h, z=1)..  ·  The electron does not radiate in an orbit.  ·  −13.6 eV is not the energy of a Balmer photon.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Balmer ends on n = 2, not n = 1.  ·  The photon energy is a difference.  ·  Name the two values of n.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A negative level energy is not the photon energy.  ·  Write E_n = −13.6 / n^2 eV and say what each symbol means.  ·  Mark the known values, then substitute one step at a time.

rows.text: Finish with the number, the unit, and the direction when the quantity has one.  ·  Four quantum numbers: n (shell), l (subshell, 0…n−1), mₗ (orientation, −l…+l), mₛ (spin ±½). Orbitals: s (spherical), p (dumbbell).  ·  State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Limit to remember: bohr model: electron in fixed circular orbits; angular momentum mvr = nh/2π; energy en = −13.6 ev·z²/n² (for h, z=1).  ·  The model gives the hydrogen numbers and fails for atoms with several electrons.
